title: Pegylated liposomal doxorubicin · every 4 weeks

agents.name: Pegylated liposomal doxorubicin
agents.explanation: Doxorubicin is carried inside tiny coated fat particles called liposomes. This changes how it circulates and its side-effect pattern. Heart injury remains possible; skin and mouth effects are especially important.
agents.watch: Report painful palms / soles or mouth ulcers early. Keep heart-test appointments and report breathlessness, swelling or chest symptoms; tell staff immediately about an infusion reaction.
risks: Mouth soreness or ulcers affecting eating and drinking
Low blood counts, infection, fatigue and nausea
Heart damage and infusion reactions; risk depends partly on previous treatment

context_label: Source-defined advanced breast, ovarian, endometrial cancer or soft-tissue sarcoma
purpose: The aim is to control the cancer and its symptoms. The team reviews benefit, side effects and your priorities before continuing.
schedule_summary: Pegylated liposomal doxorubicin on Day 1 every 28 days, typically for six cycles or until progression or unacceptable toxicity. The team confirms the intended duration and reviews benefit.

phases_title: Treatment, reassessment and the next decision
phases_note: This card describes one active chemotherapy schedule. There is no automatic maintenance phase; continuing, changing or stopping treatment follows clinical review.
timeline_note: Treatment markers show the planned days. Symptom bands show broad possibilities, not measured risk curves or guaranteed symptom-free days.
safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell needs prompt advice on any day, including planned treatment-free weeks.
teachback: Which days are treatment days, what checks are due before the next dose, and who is arranging and reviewing the next scan?
consent_support: Discuss the exact indication, expected benefit, alternatives, uncertainty, serious and lasting risks, contraception and fertility, venous access, monitoring and the urgent contact plan. This is the pegylated liposomal formulation (for example Caelyx), not conventional doxorubicin or non-pegylated Myocet. These formulations and doses must not be interchanged.
urgent_extra: Report new cough or breathlessness, fever or sudden illness promptly. Tell staff immediately about an infusion reaction or pain at the infusion site. Painful palms / soles or mouth ulcers should be reported before the next dose.

support.title: Supportive medicines
support.text: No routine premedicines are specified. Low-risk antiemetic support is separate. Infusion reactions may require a different supervised plan for future doses.

support.title: Everyday care
support.text: Use skin care advised by your team; avoid heat, friction and tight shoes for 4–7 days after infusion. Report painful palms / soles or mouth ulcers early.

support.title: Tests and appointments
support.text: Ask who books each test, when it is due and who reviews the result. Tell the team if an expected appointment has not arrived.

support.title: Correct medicine and schedule
support.text: This is the pegylated liposomal formulation (for example Caelyx), not conventional doxorubicin or non-pegylated Myocet. These formulations and doses must not be interchanged.

questions.q: Which treatment days and breaks should I expect?
questions.a: Pegylated liposomal doxorubicin on Day 1 every 28 days, typically for six cycles or until progression or unacceptable toxicity. The team confirms the intended duration and reviews benefit.

questions.q: When do I need blood tests, an ECG or echo?
questions.a: FBC, renal and liver profile before starting and before each 28-day cycle. Check mouth soreness, palms / soles and recovery from earlier toxicity before each dose. ECG is part of baseline and regular monitoring. The NCCP source advises frequent ECG monitoring; the team should specify when it is due rather than assuming an arbitrary cycle interval. Baseline echo / MUGA is required. Repeat during treatment as clinically indicated, and before each additional administration that exceeds a lifetime cumulative anthracycline exposure of 450 mg/m². Prior anthracyclines count; this threshold is not an automatic treatment stop.

questions.q: When will we know whether treatment is helping?
questions.a: For metastatic breast cancer, ESMO recommends response evaluation generally every 2–4 months, adjusted to disease, treatment and symptoms. Agree the scan type, due window and result-review appointment; symptoms can prompt earlier assessment. For the other cancer indications on this card, use the cancer-specific monitoring plan; the breast interval is not transferred automatically.

questions.q: Where do surgery or radiotherapy fit?
questions.a: These are advanced-disease regimens. Surgery or radiotherapy is used only for a defined local or symptom-control purpose. The oncology and radiation teams decide whether chemotherapy continues, pauses or precedes radiation; no routine overlap is implied.
Tumour markers, when useful for the cancer being treated, supplement clinical assessment and imaging. A marker result alone should not determine treatment failure or a treatment change.

questions.q: Does a port mean a pump at home?
questions.a: No. A port is a route into a vein. Staff disconnect the infusion and remove the port needle after the visit when appropriate; removal of the implanted device is a separate planned procedure.

evidence.title: O'Brien phase III: PLD versus conventional doxorubicin in metastatic breast cancer
evidence.intro: Evidence belongs to the cancer, population and schedule actually studied.
evidence.population: 509 women with metastatic breast cancer and normal cardiac function receiving first-line chemotherapy; PLD 50 mg/m² every four weeks versus conventional doxorubicin 60 mg/m² every three weeks.
evidence.interpretation: Comparable progression-free survival with less cardiotoxicity for PLD, while hand-foot syndrome and oral toxicity were more frequent. Overall survival was similar. Breast-trial findings do not establish efficacy in every NCCP 00205 cross-cancer indication. Normal cardiac function was required in this trial; lower cardiotoxicity does not mean cardiac safety in established heart disease or removal of monitoring. Do not interchange pegylated liposomal, non-pegylated liposomal and conventional doxorubicin.

items.text: Metastatic breast cancer; advanced ovarian cancer after failed first-line platinum chemotherapy; metastatic soft-tissue sarcoma; or recurrent / advanced endometrial cancer. Eligibility differs by cancer type.

items.text: DEXA is not a routine test for this chemotherapy alone. Assess fracture risk and bone density when indicated by endocrine treatment, ovarian suppression or other clinical risks; repeat according to the relevant plan.

chronology_notes.title: A delay changes the treatment plan
chronology_notes.text: Do not move, double or make up doses yourself. A delayed infusion does not automatically move an already-due scan or heart test.

chronology_notes.title: Review milestone
chronology_notes.text: Before every cycle, review mouth / skin recovery and cumulative anthracycline exposure; use the agreed cancer-specific response-assessment plan.

logistics.title: Your infusion and access plan
logistics.intro: Pegylated liposomal doxorubicin on Day 1 every 28 days, typically for six cycles or until progression or unacceptable toxicity. The team confirms the intended duration and reviews benefit.

steps.title: Before the first visit
steps.text: Confirm the indication, baseline bloods, required cardiac checks, medicines review and consent before the first infusion.

steps.title: Plan venous access
steps.text: A cannula, PICC or implanted port may be used. If a port is chosen, a trained team inserts it in a separate procedure with local anaesthetic and sometimes sedation; the team explains fasting, blood-thinner and wound instructions.

steps.title: Infusion day
steps.text: The first infusion starts at 1 mg per minute. Later infusions may take 60 minutes if there was no reaction; a previous reaction requires a modified supervised schedule. Staff observe for reactions. Report burning, pain, swelling or leakage at the infusion site immediately.

steps.title: Home and next review
steps.text: This regimen does not routinely need a take-home infusion pump. Staff disconnect the infusion; a port is de-accessed when appropriate. Keep line-care and next-visit instructions.

details.title: Port insertion and removal
details.text: The line team explains placement, dressing care and when normal activities can resume. A port is accessed with a special needle during treatment. Removal of the implanted device is a separate planned procedure when no longer needed; do not remove or adjust it yourself.

details.title: PICC care and urgent line symptoms
details.text: A PICC usually needs regular dressing and flushing appointments even between treatments. Fever, redness, swelling, pain, leakage or damage requires prompt advice. Your hospital supplies the exact care instructions.

details.title: Visit length
details.text: The first infusion starts at 1 mg per minute. Later infusions may take 60 minutes if there was no reaction; a previous reaction requires a modified supervised schedule. A port is optional access, not a requirement for a take-home pump. This regimen has no routine ambulatory pump.

details.title: Premedication
details.text: No routine premedicines are specified. Low-risk antiemetic support is separate. Infusion reactions may require a different supervised plan for future doses.

anatomy: Report painful redness, swelling or peeling early.
